citations.assessment: Avot 3:12 names bare Yishmael.
Avot 4:5 and 4:7 both give Yishmael his son. Preserve the relational wording and check the antecedent and gloss witnesses before assigning this material to the undesignated Yishmael.
Yishmael gives the formula for communal invitation to bless.
Yishmael assigns stalks from the hand and sickle to the poor, against Akiva.
Yishmael gives the second tithe to the Jerusalemite landowner.
Yishmael requires the furrow to run across the field.
Yishmael proposes uprooting two rows and planting one; Akiva differs.
Meir and Yose both transmit in Yishmael’s name with divergent area measures.
Yehoshua visits Yishmael in Kefar Aziz and asks about planting under the vine.
Yishmael distinguishes optional harvest from the omer harvest.
Yishmael gives the half ordinary, half terumah ruling.
Yishmael describes the qualifying Tyrian courtyard.
Yishmael takes challah from the middle of the joined new and old lots.
Yishmael forbids tar for Sabbath lighting on grounds of Sabbath honor.
Yishmael permits preparing garments and beds on Yom Kippur for Shabbat and distinguishes the sacrifices.
A student reports a view in Yishmael’s name before Akiva.
Separate blessing for the festival offering does not discharge the Passover blessing in Yishmael’s view.
Yishmael gives Greek names on the baskets.
Yishmael permits purchasing wine, oil and flour with surplus and retaining the profit for the sanctuary. Yishmael distinguishes surplus produce from surplus of collected funds.
Yishmael says the priest only needed to pronounce the divine designation.
Yishmael reports the crimson thread as a sign the goat had reached the wilderness.
Yishmael specifies the numbers and condition of the four species.
Yose identifies the barley allotment with Yishmael living near Edom.
Yishmael cites thirteen covenants for circumcision.
Narrative of the niece’s vow, her treatment and the lament on Yishmael’s death.
Yishmael forbids rubbing with earth because it loosens hair.
R. Yishmael sets the eighteen-month rule for a grain field and three productive periods for an orchard.
His objection to Akiva compares the smaller building to a cattle shed.
He assigns payment from unencumbered property, debates the guarantor’s case, and praises studying civil law.
A teaching in his name requires twenty-three judges for lashes.
The doubled concealment makes both unawareness of impurity and of Temple liability actionable.
He restricts the oath offering to future acts and debates Akiva on the verse’s expansion.

Three opinions before the sages at Yavneh, on the beaten egg, the stalk and the garden. Three questions posed before him, with no ruling from him and explanation by Yehoshua ben Matya. The block introduces three opinions rejected by Akiva, with the first on completing mashed foods after dark.
Lists three leniencies of Shammai and stringencies of Hillel, including Qohelet.
He forbids transactions before and after the festivals, unlike the Sages’ one-sided interval.
He questions Yehoshua about cheese and the ensuing verse reading.
He distinguishes three and two stones by a Mercurius shrine.
He counts the fringes as four commandments.
His omer measure varies by Sabbath versus weekday.
His two half-olive portions on a hide convey impurity by carrying, but not contact.
He gives species-specific ages and disputes Akiva about assurance of first birth.
He uses the number of sacs as evidence for two testes.
He describes the condition listed as the largest blemish.
He explains the wording as crushed testes, distinct from Akiva and Chanina.
Reconciling two verses, permits dedicating a firstling for valuation but not for altar dedication.
Identifies the designated woman as entirely enslaved, against other interpretations.
Contrasts the changing liability for sacred misuse of blood and libations.
Gives vessel capacity-based thresholds for earthenware fragments.
Purifies where Meir allows impurity by contact.
Uses a skewer lowered vertically to mark the airspace.
Requires a quarter-log before and one after death with one combined sample.
Compares reddish whiteness to blood mixed with milk.
Uses boxwood as the intermediate comparison for judging Israelite skin.
Treats the return of uncovered extremities like that in a large bright patch.
Orders washing and seclusion for an initially faded patch.
Four stones and the required appearance size, against Akiva’s eight and two-stone requirement.
Names the intermediate-age ram parchedigma.
Uses stone pounding implements and stone sieves.
Requires waiting for cloudy water to settle.
Differentiates the timing for the two cases in the pregnancy ruling.
Sets a hair threshold by ability to bend the tip to the root.
The second-day sighting invalidates the prior day.
Akiva reports his opposition about snow and testimony in his name permitting it for a new immersion pool.
Ranges from four to six periods, against Akiva’s five.
A one-sided stain also interposes, according to Yehudah in his name.
Places the burden of proof on Elazar ben Azaryah as the more stringent party.
Counts the feathers toward the aggregate.
Treats the single-side covering as if it surrounded the food like a ring.

Maimonides explicitly says student of Akiva despite ruling like Yishmael.
The cited codification actually appears in the Book of Times, Hilkhot Shabbat 5:10; preserve Heilprin’s Madda locator and distinguish the ruling from the biographical assertion.
Tarfon introduces the visit of four elders and warns the others not to interrupt, and Yishmael says he burdened his teachers more than once.
Yishmael tells the listeners to tell Akiva he erred, in the case of inference by analogy.
Davidson gives Yishmael as the one sending the rebuke to Akiva in the manna dispute.

Yehoshua faults Yishmael’s position on prior births and visible signs.
Yishmael praises civil law and commends Shimon ben Nannas; the recommendation does not establish formal discipleship.

citations.assessment: Matya asks Azaryah about Yishmael’s four divisions; the answer treats repentance together with three.
Yishmael hears Nechunya, and Akiva hears Nachum of Gam Zu. This supports the inherited parenthetical correction.
The Bavli and Mishnah give Yehoshua as respondent. This textual finding does not independently verify Rabbenu Chananel’s formulation.
Rashi explicitly cites the cheese conversation with Yehoshua responding.
The selected Midrash Rabbah includes the address my brother and says Yishmael was young.

Kefar Aziz and Yehoshua’s visit are explicit; keep Ḥaziz as the parallel variant.
Shekalim names Yishmael and Akiva jointly.

citations.assessment: Davidson reads מיוזנת; Rashi explains the comparison to a shop with wine always ready. The phrase does not describe weapons.
The Ḥullin text preserves Ben Azzai's regret.

The Daat witness prints (Akiva) [Yehoshua] and marks 'my brother' parenthetically. The witness preserves both names.
The indexed Yerushalmi says that R. Yishmael was young at the time.
